section.title: The Song of the Vineyard
section.sectionRationale: This movement opens with a love song turned lawsuit, God's meticulous care for His vineyard, Israel, answered only with wild grapes, and moves into a series of six woes naming specific sins, greed, drunkenness, moral inversion, self-conceit, corrupt justice, until the chapter closes with a foreign army summoned as the LORD's own instrument of judgment. It is the seam where general indictment becomes an itemized charge sheet.
section.thesis: The LORD lavished everything on His vineyard, Israel, expecting justice and righteousness, but found only bloodshed and the cry of the oppressed, so He names their specific sins one by one and summons a swift, relentless army to execute the judgment His patience has finally exhausted.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the song of the vineyard and its bitter fruit; six woes naming Israel's specific sins; and the LORD's whistle for a distant nation, summoned like a lion to devour.

units.label: The song of the vineyard
units.note: wild grapes instead of good fruit

verses.text:
I will sing for my beloved a song of his vineyard: 
My beloved had a {{kerem|vineyard}} on a very fertile hill.

He dug it up and cleared the stones and planted the finest vines. He built a watchtower in the middle and dug out a winepress as well. 
He waited for the vineyard to yield good grapes, but the fruit it produced was sour!
“And now, O dwellers of Jerusalem and men of Judah, I exhort you to judge between Me and My vineyard.
What more could I have done for My vineyard than I already did for it? Why, when I expected sweet grapes, did it bring forth sour fruit?

Now I will tell you what I am about to do to My vineyard: 
I will take away its hedge, and it will be consumed; I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled.

I will make it a wasteland, neither pruned nor cultivated, 
and thorns and briers will grow up. I will command the clouds that rain shall not fall on it.”

For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight. He looked for {{mishpat2|justice}}, but saw bloodshed; for {{tzedaqah2|righteousness}}, but heard a cry of distress.
Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you live alone in the land.

I heard the LORD of Hosts declare: 
“Surely many houses will become desolate, great mansions left unoccupied.
For ten acres of vineyard will yield but a bath of wine, and a homer of seed only an ephah of grain. ”
Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink, who linger into the evening, to be inflamed by wine.
At their feasts are the lyre and harp, tambourines and flutes and wine. They disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands.
Therefore My people will go into exile for their lack of understanding; their dignitaries are starving and their masses are parched with thirst.
Therefore Sheol enlarges its throat and opens wide its enormous jaws, and down go Zion's nobles and masses, her revelers and carousers!
So mankind will be brought low, and each man humbled; the arrogant will lower their eyes.
But the LORD of Hosts will be exalted by His justice, and the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness.
Lambs will graze as in their own pastures, and strangers will feed in the ruins of the wealthy.
Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of deceit and pull sin along with cart ropes,
to those who say, “Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it! Let the plan of the Holy One of Israel come so that we may know it!”
Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who turn darkness to light and light to darkness, who replace bitter with sweet and sweet with bitter.
Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight.
Woe to those who are heroes in drinking wine and champions in mixing beer,
who acquit the guilty for a bribe and deprive the innocent of justice.

Therefore, as a tongue of fire consumes the straw, and as dry grass shrivels in the flame, so their roots will decay and their blossoms will blow away like dust; for they have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.

units.label: The LORD whistles for a distant nation
units.note: an army summoned like a lion

verses.text:
Therefore the anger of the LORD burns against His people; His hand is raised against them to strike them down. The mountains quake, and the corpses lay like refuse in the streets. 
Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.

He lifts a banner for the distant nations and whistles for those at the ends of the earth. 
Behold, how speedily and swiftly they come!
None of them grows weary or stumbles; no one slumbers or sleeps. No belt is loose and no sandal strap is broken.
Their arrows are sharpened, and all their bows are strung. The hooves of their horses are like flint; their chariot wheels are like a whirlwind.
Their roaring is like that of a lion; they roar like young lions. They growl and seize their prey; they carry it away from deliverance.

In that day they will roar over it, like the roaring of the sea. If one looks over the land, he will see darkness and distress; 
even the light will be obscured by clouds.

kerem.gloss: Vineyard, a common Old Testament image for Israel as the object of God's careful cultivation and love. Everything about the vineyard here, the fertile hill, cleared stones, finest vines, watchtower, and winepress, pictures lavish, deliberate care that makes the resulting wild grapes all the more shocking.

mishpat2.gloss: Justice, the right ordering of community life. Verse 7 turns on a devastating Hebrew wordplay: God looked for mishpat, justice, but found mispach, bloodshed, sounds that are nearly identical in Hebrew, driving home how close true justice was replaced by its violent counterfeit.

tzedaqah2.gloss: Righteousness, right conduct and right relationship. The same verse plays on tzedaqah versus tze'aqah, a cry of distress, another near-rhyme in Hebrew, so the vineyard's fruit is the very opposite, in sound and substance, of what was planted.

basic.context: Isaiah sings what sounds like a love song about a vineyard lovingly prepared on a fertile hill, only to reveal partway through that the vineyard is Israel and the disappointing fruit is Judah's injustice and violence. The chapter then lists six specific woes, greed for land, drunken indifference, moral inversion, self-conceit, and corrupt courts, before ending with God summoning a foreign army as swift and relentless as a lion to execute judgment.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real indictment of real social sins in eighth century Judah, using a beloved song form to disarm the hearers before the twist reveals they are the guilty vineyard, a rhetorical strategy similar to Nathan's parable to David in 2 Samuel 12. The uncomfortable question the chapter raises is why God would use a foreign, pagan army as His own instrument; the answer running through Isaiah is that God is sovereign over every nation and can wield even Israel's enemies for His righteous purposes.
basic.originalLanguages: God's vineyard, kerem, receives every possible advantage, yet yields wild grapes instead of good fruit. The devastating point of verse 7 is a Hebrew wordplay: God sought mishpat, justice, but found mispach, bloodshed, and looked for tzedaqah, righteousness, but heard tze'aqah, a cry of distress, near-identical sounds exposing how far the fruit had twisted from what was planted.
basic.typology: The vineyard given every advantage yet yielding wild grapes anticipates Jesus's own parable of the vineyard and the wicked tenants, Matthew 21:33-41, where the LORD of the vineyard finally sends His own Son. The lion-like army summoned from the ends of the earth foreshadows how God remains sovereign over every nation, even hostile ones, using them within His larger redemptive purposes.
basic.christ: Jesus deliberately picks up Isaiah's vineyard image in His own parable of the wicked tenants, Matthew 21:33-46, alluding directly to this song, but pushes it further: rather than merely disciplining an unfruitful vineyard, God sends His own beloved Son into it, and is rejected and killed, yet becomes the cornerstone of a new, fruitful people. Christ is also the true and faithful Israel who, unlike the vineyard here, produced the justice and righteousness the Father sought.
basic.god: God is pictured as a devoted vinedresser, doing everything possible for His people, which makes their unfaithfulness all the more inexcusable and His subsequent judgment all the more just rather than arbitrary. Yet even in summoning judgment, God remains sovereign over history's nations, showing that His justice operates on a scale far larger than Israel alone.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Samuel 12:1-7 uses a similarly disarming parable to expose David's own sin before pronouncing judgment. Psalm 80:8-16 also pictures Israel as a vine God brought out of Egypt and later broke down. Matthew 21:33-46 directly develops Isaiah's vineyard song into the parable of the wicked tenants. Habakkuk 1:5-11 likewise wrestles with God raising up a fierce foreign nation as an instrument of judgment.
basic.oneStory: The Song of the Vineyard pictures the whole story of God's patient, lavish care for His people met again and again with unfaithfulness, a pattern Jesus Himself invokes when He tells of a vineyard owner who finally sends his own son. The story's resolution is not another failed vineyard but the true Vine, Christ, who bears the fruit Israel could not, John 15:1-5.

context.literary:
Chapter 5 is built in three panels, and the speaker changes in each. In verses 1 and 2 Isaiah sings in the first person about 'my beloved' and his vineyard, in the voice of a friend at a harvest celebration. In verses 3 to 6 the voice quietly becomes the owner's own, 'judge between Me and My vineyard,' and the hearers are invited to act as jurors in a case that, they think, concerns someone else. Verse 7 steps outside the song and names the vineyard, so the verdict they would have reached on a stranger falls on them. Nathan used the same trap on David, 2 Samuel 12:1-7, and the song works only because it is told as a story before it is heard as an accusation.

The second panel is structured by one cry. The word 'Woe' opens verses 8, 11, 18, 20, 21 and 22, six times, and the sins move from the economy (land grabbing) to the feast (drink, music, and no eye for the LORD's work), to defiant talk (cords of deceit, 'Let Him hurry'), to a collapse of moral vocabulary (evil called good), to pride, and finally to the courtroom. Two 'therefore' clauses answer the first two woes in verses 13 to 17, and a third, in verse 24, answers the rest. Verse 16 sits like a pivot in the midst of the ruin: the LORD of Hosts 'will be exalted by His justice.'

The third panel does not end with the chapter. The refrain of verse 25, 'Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised,' returns word for word at Isaiah 9:12, 9:17, 9:21 and 10:4, so chapter 5 is the opening stanza of a poem whose remaining stanzas are scattered through the next five chapters. The closing image is also a quiet reversal of verse 20. Those who 'turn darkness to light' end up in a land of 'darkness and distress,' with even the light 'obscured by clouds.'
context.historical:
The song belongs to the long, prosperous reigns of Uzziah and Jotham, when Judah was wealthy, secure and spiritually careless. The land laws of Israel had been designed to prevent exactly what verse 8 describes. Land was not a commodity: 'The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine,' Leviticus 25:23, and each family held an inheritance in trust. Isaiah's younger contemporary Micah describes the same practice in the same breath, 'They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses,' Micah 2:2. Those who joined 'house to house and field to field' were using debt and the courts to dissolve the tribal inheritance until one landlord 'live[d] alone in the land.' The result in verse 10 is a harvest failure so severe that ten acres of vineyard, by the BSB footnote the work of ten yoke of oxen in a day, yield about twenty two litres of wine, and a homer of seed returns an ephah, a tenth of what was sown.

The feasts of verse 12 belong to the same culture of ease. Amos, working in the north at the same period, pictures the elite on ivory couches who 'improvise songs on the harp like David' while failing 'to grieve over the ruin of Joseph,' Amos 6:4-6. Isaiah's charge is not that music or wine is wrong, but that the revellers 'disregard the actions of the LORD,' so they cannot read the signs of an approaching empire.

That empire is Assyria. Under Tiglath-pileser III it had been marching west since the 740s BC, and the nation 'at the ends of the earth' of verse 26 is a description from Judah's point of view of a power that was in fact only a few years away. Assyria is not named here; by Isaiah 7:17 and 8:7 it is. The summons is given in military signals, a banner raised on a hill and a whistle, the way a commander gathers troops. The 'mountains quake' of verse 25 may recall the earthquake of Uzziah's day, Amos 1:1, though the text does not say so.
context.canonical:
Israel as a vine is one of the Bible's oldest pictures. Psalm 80:8-16 recalls the vine brought out of Egypt and planted in cleared ground, and then asks why its walls were broken down, which is exactly the fate Isaiah announces in verse 5. Hosea 10:1 says 'Israel was a luxuriant vine, yielding fruit for himself,' and the more the fruit grew, the more altars were built. Jeremiah 2:21 turns the Isaiah image into a direct reproach: 'I had planted you like a choice vine from the very best seed. How could you turn yourself before Me into a rotten, wild vine?' Each prophet reaches for the same picture because the Torah and the Psalms had already supplied it.

Isaiah himself comes back to the vineyard. In Isaiah 27:2-6 the song is sung again 'in that day,' and the verdict is reversed: 'I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually,' and 'Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit.' Chapter 5 is therefore not the last word on the vineyard, only the first.

The woes echo across the prophets. Habakkuk 2:6-9 gives a series of woes to the one who 'amasses what is not his,' and the structure is a taunt song in the manner of Isaiah 5. Jesus takes the form into the New Testament. In Matthew 23:13-15 He pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees, and in Luke 6:24-26 on the rich, the well fed and those spoken well of. His parable of the tenants, Matthew 21:33-44 and Luke 20:9-19, rebuilds the song from the inside, and in John 15:1-8 He says, 'I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard.' The vineyard image runs from the Exodus to the upper room.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted Judah to hear the verdict before they knew it was about them. A prophet who opens an indictment with an accusation gets argument in return; a prophet who sings a love song gets a hearing. By the time the hearers have agreed that the owner has done all he could, they have already signed the finding against themselves, verse 3. The song's first purpose is therefore to remove the excuse of ignorance and of divine neglect: nothing was left undone, verse 4.

The woes are meant to be taken as a plain list of what 'sour fruit' looks like in daily life. Isaiah does not call for rituals here; he names a way of using land, a way of spending evenings, a way of speaking about God, a way of reasoning about good and evil, and a way of running courts. Justice and righteousness are measured in the village, the winepress and the gate, not in the temple.

He also wanted his hearers to grasp that the delay of judgment is not its cancellation. Verse 19 quotes the mockers who say, 'Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it,' which treats the LORD's patience as proof that He will do nothing. The closing scene answers that taunt with an army that never tires. The people who asked to see the plan of the Holy One of Israel are shown it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes God's own judgment on a specific society; it does not give believers a script for calling disasters down on their neighbours. The vineyard's fate in verses 5 and 6 and the army of verses 26 to 30 are statements about what the LORD will do, not instructions. Reading every modern war or drought as a precise judgment on a particular sin goes far beyond what Isaiah claims, and Jesus warns against it in Luke 13:1-5.

What does carry forward are the moral categories. Greed that treats land and housing as a way to be alone, pleasure that leaves no room to notice God at work, the relabelling of evil as good, self-congratulating cleverness and bought verdicts are named as sin, and the New Testament shares that judgment: see Romans 12:16 on conceit and Proverbs 3:7, 'Be not wise in your own eyes.' The song also teaches a standard of fruit. God looks for justice and righteousness in His people's life together, and Jesus says that the kingdom will be given to those 'who will produce its fruit,' Matthew 21:43. Believers are not told to earn their place in the vine, but they are told that a branch that bears nothing is not an ornament, John 15:2.

debates.question: Who is the 'beloved' of verse 1, and what kind of song is it?

views.label: Isaiah sings as the bridegroom's friend
views.case: The opening reads like a wedding or harvest song in which a friend sings on behalf of 'my beloved.' This reading explains the tender, narrative tone of verses 1 and 2, and it fits the way verse 3 swings into the owner's own voice without warning. The beloved is the LORD, and the vineyard is His bride-like possession, as in Hosea 2.

views.label: A parable that is a lawsuit in disguise
views.case: Others stress verse 3, where Judah is asked to 'judge,' and verse 4, 'What more could I have done,' as the language of a court dispute. The song is then a rib, a covenant lawsuit, as in Isaiah 1:2-3, dressed in love song form. The legal reading explains why the verdict in verse 7 is stated as a charge: justice and bloodshed, righteousness and a cry.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: The mixed voices and the shift from tenderness to indictment suggest that Isaiah deliberately used the form of a love song to make a legal case. The listeners expect a celebration and receive a verdict. Many readers now accept that the genre is hybrid on purpose.

debates.bearing: The disagreement is mostly about genre, not meaning. Either way the song makes the same two points: the LORD's care for Israel was complete, and the failure was theirs. It also shows the risk in hearing a story about God's care without letting it search us.

debates.question: How should we read the army of verses 26 to 30, and why is it unnamed?

views.label: Assyria, seen from Judah's horizon
views.case: The summons of a distant nation, the banner and the whistle, fit Assyria's westward advance in the late eighth century, and Isaiah 7:17-20, 8:7 and 10:5-6 name Assyria as the LORD's instrument. Isaiah 10:5 calls Assyria 'the rod of My anger,' which matches the language of verse 25, the upraised hand.

views.label: A deliberately open picture
views.case: Isaiah leaves the army nameless, and later prophets use the same language of a nation from afar for other powers, such as the Chaldeans in Habakkuk 1:6-8 and the curse of Deuteronomy 28:49-50. On this view the passage describes the pattern, a distant, tireless, merciless nation, so that any later instrument of judgment fits it.

views.label: Assyria first, and then the pattern recurs
views.case: The first reading and the second can be combined: Isaiah has Assyria in mind, and the details were then reused for Babylon and, at the last, for the great day of the LORD in the New Testament.

debates.bearing: The chapter's own focus is not the identity of the army but who is behind it: it is the LORD who lifts the banner and whistles. That conviction explains why Isaiah can later say that the instrument will be judged for its own arrogance, Isaiah 10:12-15.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 names the singer's friend with the Hebrew word yedid, 'beloved,' from the same family as dod, the word for a lover in the Song of Songs. The vineyard is 'a vineyard of fertility,' literally on a 'horn of oil,' keren ben shamen, a hill shaped like a horn and rich in oil. The words are chosen to prepare a love song and to make the reversal hit harder.

The sour fruit of verse 2 is be'ushim. The word is not a gentle one: it comes from a root associated with stench, and it means rotten or foul fruit rather than merely unripe fruit. Isaiah uses a word for the opposite of what the owner wanted, 'good grapes,' anavim. The question in verse 4 repeats the same pair, so the contrast stays in the ear.

The verbs of verse 2 are a vineyard-builder's checklist, and the Hebrew gives them in a crisp series: he dug it, cleared it of stones, planted it with choice vines (sorek), built a tower, and hewed out a winepress. The vine called sorek is the choice red vine, and Jeremiah 2:21 uses the same word when he says God planted Israel as a 'choice vine.' The care was thorough, down to the kind of vine, which is why Jeremiah can speak of 'the very best seed.'

The word 'woe,' hoy, is a cry from the funeral. In 1 Kings 13:30 the mourners lament over a dead prophet with 'Oh, my brother!' The woes of chapter 5 are therefore laments sung for people who are still alive, a graveside speech given before the death. It announces that the road you are on ends in the grave.

In verse 14 Sheol 'enlarges its throat,' using nephesh, a word that can mean throat or appetite. The underworld is pictured as having an appetite, and it is the revellers who feed it. The drinkers' 'appetite' for wine in verse 11 is answered by Sheol's appetite for them.

In verse 20 the three inversions, evil for good, darkness for light, bitter for sweet, mirror the creation vocabulary of Genesis 1, where God divides light from darkness and pronounces what is good, Genesis 1:3-4. Isaiah describes the unmaking of that moral order.

The refrain of verse 25 uses the verb natah, 'stretched out.' It is the verb of the stretched out arm in the Exodus, but here it stretches out against Israel. The same hand that once drew Israel out of Egypt is raised against her.

typology.type: The vineyard and its keeper, Isaiah 5:1-7
typology.fulfillment: Israel as God's planted vine is a pattern that the New Testament takes up and sharpens. Jesus says in John 15:1, 'I am the true vine,' and the Father is the keeper of the vineyard. Where Israel as a vine produced be'ushim, Christ is the vine whose fruit is exactly what the owner sought. His people bear fruit by remaining in Him, John 15:4-5, so the fruit that Israel could not produce becomes possible. The type falls short because Israel's vine could be uprooted and abandoned, whereas the true vine cannot fail, though branches that do not remain are cut off, John 15:2.

typology.type: The vineyard tower and wall, Isaiah 5:2, 5
typology.fulfillment: The tower and winepress of the song reappear as the furniture of Jesus's parable, Matthew 21:33, which adds a new feature, tenants who kill the owner's servants and finally his son, Matthew 21:35-39. The hedge and wall were the owner's protection, and verse 5 shows what happens when they are removed. The fulfilment is that the protection is not withdrawn without a last appeal: God sends His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2. The type is limited because the song's owner never sends anyone, but the parable's owner sends servants and then his beloved son.

typology.type: The summoned army as the LORD's instrument, Isaiah 5:26-30
typology.fulfillment: God uses a distant nation to carry out His judgment, whistling for them. The pattern recurs when Rome destroys Jerusalem in the generation after Christ, and Jesus foresees it in Luke 19:43-44 and Luke 21:20-24, because Jerusalem 'did not recognize the time of your visitation from God,' Luke 19:44. The final form of the pattern is the day when the rulers of the earth hide from 'the wrath of the Lamb,' Revelation 6:15-17. The type has limits: the instruments in Isaiah act from their own pride, Isaiah 10:7, while the final judgment is carried out by Christ Himself.

study.christ:
The song leads to Christ most directly through His own use of it. When Jesus tells the parable of the tenants in Matthew 21:33-44, He borrows nearly every feature of Isaiah 5:1-2, the planted vineyard, the wall, the winepress and the tower, so His hearers could not miss the allusion. What He adds is the new element that Isaiah's song lacks. In the song the owner asks, 'What more could I have done?' The parable's answer is that there was one more thing: 'Finally, he sent his son to them,' Matthew 21:37. The last appeal of the vineyard's owner is the incarnation. Luke even makes the owner say, 'I will send my beloved son,' Luke 20:13, and the word 'beloved' echoes the opening word of Isaiah's song, 'my beloved.'

Jesus then quotes Psalm 118: 'The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,' Matthew 21:42, and warns that 'he on whom it falls will be crushed,' Matthew 21:44. Luke records that the scribes and chief priests 'realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them,' Luke 20:19, just as Isaiah's hearers were meant to realize that the vineyard was themselves. The verdict of Matthew 21:43, that the kingdom 'will be given to a people who will produce its fruit,' is the New Testament counterpart of Isaiah 5:5-6, with the promise that the vineyard will not be abandoned for good. Isaiah 27:2-6 had already promised that the LORD would sing the vineyard song again, with a happier ending.

He is also the answer to the missing fruit. The song shows that the problem lay in the vine, not in the care. What Israel could not produce, the true vine does: 'I am the true vine,' John 15:1. In Him the fruit of justice and righteousness that the owner sought is finally found in a human life. Paul can later say that believers are 'filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ,' Philippians 1:11.

Christ also takes the woes upon Himself in one sense. He pronounces the same woes on the religious elite, Matthew 23, and weeps over the city that will fall, Luke 19:41-44. The Judge who pronounces the verdict is the One who suffers its consequence, outside the walls, Hebrews 13:12.

A caution is in order. The vineyard is Israel in Isaiah, and it is not a code for every church or every nation. The song does not itself mention the Son. The link rests on the way Jesus reshapes the song, and on the New Testament's use of the vine, rather than on a hidden prediction in every detail of the vineyard.
study.god:
The song shows a God who gives with both hands. The list of verses 1 and 2 is the biography of a patient labourer, who digs, clears, plants, builds and waits, and the point is that the vineyard did not fail from neglect. God's care is never the weak link. When He asks, 'What more could I have done?' in verse 4, He is not confessing a lack but inviting an honest verdict. This is a God who lets His own conduct be examined by the very people who stand accused, and who can bear the examination.

He is a God of expectation. Verse 7 says He 'looked for' justice and righteousness. The God who knows everything is spoken of as looking for fruit, which is the language of a covenant partner, not a spectator. Because He has a right to expect something, the lack of it is a real offence against Him and a real wound to the poor whose 'cry of distress' is heard, verse 7. The word translated 'cry' is the word used of the outcry of the oppressed in Egypt, so the God who heard Israel's cry now hears it from Israel's own victims.

He is holy, and that holiness is what judgment protects. Verse 16 says that 'the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness.' This is not a harsh addition to His love; it is the same character. A holy God cannot treat the crushing of the poor as ordinary. Isaiah's title for Him, 'the Holy One of Israel,' is used in this chapter both for the Judge and for the One whose word was despised, verses 19 and 24.

He is sovereign over the nations. Verses 25 to 30 show that the world's armies answer a whistle. He lifts the banner, He calls, and the army comes. This is not the picture of a God who is caught off guard by history. Yet the same chapter keeps the human responsibility intact: nobody in the song is told they were forced to produce sour fruit.

He is patient and yet not endlessly so. Verse 25's 'His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised' shows judgment coming in waves with the hand still up, a God who has struck and is still reaching toward them. The refrain is a terrible phrase and a hopeful one, because a hand that is still upraised can still be seen, and the call to repent has not yet expired.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to receive God's gifts as a trust. The right response to the song is not to defend the vineyard but to say that the verdict is fair. The people who have learned to say that, as David did in Psalm 51:4, are the ones who can hope for the restoration of Isaiah 27.

crossReferences.note: Nathan's parable of the poor man's ewe lamb works in the same way as Isaiah's song. The listener passes judgment on a story, and the prophet then says it is about him. Both parables rely on the hearer's sense of fairness, so that the sentence is condemned from their own mouth.

The psalmist recalls the vine from Egypt that filled the land, then asks why its walls are broken down so that passers by pick its fruit. It is the prayer that Isaiah's song answers: the walls are down because the vineyard bore sour fruit, not because the owner forgot.

Jeremiah gives the same story in two lines: a choice vine planted from the best seed has become a rotten, wild vine. The wording shows that the problem is not the planting but the plant, and that Israel's turning was a turning 'before Me,' in the presence of the owner.

The song sung again 'in that day.' The LORD is now the vineyard's keeper who waters it continually and guards it night and day, and Israel will fill the world with fruit. It shows that Isaiah 5 is not God's last word on the vineyard, only the first.

Jesus reuses the vineyard, wall, winepress and tower of Isaiah 5:2, and then adds the owner's servants and his son. The chief priests and elders see that He is speaking about them. The quotation of Psalm 118 about the rejected stone turns the story from a lament into a promise of a new, fruit bearing people.

Jesus says He is the true vine and the Father the keeper of the vineyard. The fruitfulness that Israel could not give is given to those who remain in Him. It shows how the sour grapes of Isaiah 5 are answered, not by trying harder but by being joined to a different vine.

Micah, a contemporary of Isaiah, begins a woe about the same crime as Isaiah 5:8. People plot at night and carry out their plans by day because they have the power, and they 'covet fields and seize them.' Two independent prophets name the same sin, which confirms how widespread it was.

The land is the LORD's and Israel's families are residents with Him. This is the legal ground for the woe of Isaiah 5:8: adding field to field until one lives alone in the land cuts against the principle that no family may be written out of the inheritance.

Amos describes the feasting elite of the same generation, with its beds of ivory, its songs and its wine bowls, who 'fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph.' This is the same indifference as Isaiah 5:12, where the feasters 'disregard the actions of the LORD.'

The refrain of Isaiah 5:25, 'Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised,' returns here, along with the rest of the poem on the northern kingdom's pride. It shows that the end of chapter 5 is the first stanza of a longer lament about judgment that keeps arriving.

The LORD calls Assyria 'the rod of My anger,' and then says that Assyria does not know it, since its heart is only to destroy. This explains the whistle of Isaiah 5:26: the army is summoned by God, yet it will answer for its own cruelty.

Habakkuk answers the oppressor with a series of woes as a taunt song, beginning with the one who 'amasses what is not his.' The form is the same as Isaiah 5, and shows that the woe is a standard prophetic vehicle for exposing the greed that Isaiah names in verse 8.

study.oneStory:
The vineyard begins where Eden ended. In the garden the first couple were placed to work and keep, Genesis 2:15, and were put out when they did not. Isaiah 5 tells the same story at the scale of a nation: a planted place, a clear task, an owner who comes looking for fruit, and a failure that ends in exile. The vineyard is Israel's version of Genesis 3, played out in the land and in time.

The song also picks up the promise to Abraham that his family would be a blessing, Genesis 12:2-3. A blessing carries fruit with it, and the fruit God names in Isaiah is justice and righteousness. The same pair describe Abraham's own mission in Genesis 18:19, where the LORD says that Abraham is to command his household 'to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just.' When Israel produced bloodshed and a cry of distress, it betrayed the very purpose of its calling.

What follows in Isaiah is a deepening of the story. The coming exile is announced in verse 13, 'My people will go into exile for their lack of understanding,' and Isaiah 7 and 8 will name Assyria. The hope is also kept alive, for the vineyard song of Isaiah 27 and the stump and shoot of Isaiah 11:1 both belong to a God who does not abandon what He planted. The vine returns in the Psalms, Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, always in the double sense of promise and failure.

The New Testament brings the story to a point. The owner finally sends His beloved son, and the son is killed outside the vineyard, Matthew 21:39. But the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and a new people are given the kingdom, Matthew 21:42-43. Jesus is the true vine, and His people are the branches, John 15:5. They are not a replacement for Israel's story but its fruit, and Paul can describe Gentile believers as wild branches grafted into the cultivated olive, Romans 11:17-24.

The new creation is the vineyard finally yielding what the Owner sought. The ground of Genesis 3 was cursed with thorns and thistles, and the vineyard of Isaiah 5:6 is overgrown with them; in the new creation there will be 'no longer any curse,' Revelation 22:3. The cry of distress that the LORD heard in verse 7 will be answered when God wipes away every tear and justice is at last the way things are, Revelation 21:4. The people of the vineyard will 'fill the whole world with fruit,' Isaiah 27:6, and the song that began with a failure ends in a feast.

quiz.q: What is the twist revealed partway through the Song of the Vineyard?

options.text: The vineyard, lovingly prepared, is Israel and Judah, and the disappointing fruit is their injustice and violence.
options.note: Verse 7 makes the allegory explicit: the house of Israel is the LORD's vineyard.

options.text: The vineyard represents Jerusalem's physical agriculture with no symbolic meaning.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly identifies the vineyard as the house of Israel, a clear allegory.

options.text: The vineyard belongs to a foreign king, not the LORD.
options.note: The song is explicitly about 'my beloved,' God, and His own vineyard.

options.text: The vineyard produced good fruit but was destroyed anyway.
options.note: The song specifically says the vineyard produced wild, sour grapes despite every advantage.

quiz.q: What is the effect of the Hebrew wordplay in verse 7, mishpat versus mispach, tzedaqah versus tze'aqah?

options.text: It sonically underscores how completely justice was replaced by its violent, near-identical-sounding counterfeit.
options.note: The near-rhymes in Hebrew drive home the shocking reversal of what God expected versus what He found.

options.text: It shows the words are simply synonyms with no rhetorical purpose.
options.note: The pairs are opposites, justice versus bloodshed, righteousness versus distress, deliberately chosen for their similar sound.

options.text: It is a scribal error later corrected in translation.
options.note: This is a deliberate poetic device, not an error.

options.text: It only functions in English translation, not the original Hebrew.
options.note: The wordplay works specifically in the Hebrew sounds, and English translations can only describe rather than fully reproduce it.

quiz.q: What sin does the first woe, verse 8, specifically condemn?

options.text: Greedily accumulating houses and fields until small landholders are pushed out entirely.
options.note: This reflects the real economic exploitation of small farmers by the wealthy in Isaiah's day.

options.text: Refusing to own any property at all.
options.note: The woe condemns excessive accumulation, not the absence of property.

options.text: Failing to pay agricultural taxes.
options.note: The text names land consolidation and displacement of others, not tax evasion specifically.

options.text: Building too many watchtowers for defense.
options.note: The woe is about houses and fields being joined together, not military structures.

quiz.q: What does the woe in verse 20, calling evil good and good evil, describe?

options.text: A moral inversion where society's basic categories of right and wrong have been reversed.
options.note: This is one of the most quoted verses on moral relativism and confusion.

options.text: Simple disagreement about minor matters of preference.
options.note: The verse describes a fundamental inversion of moral categories, not mere preference.

options.text: A description of colorblindness.
options.note: Darkness and light, bitter and sweet, are metaphors for moral categories, not physical vision.

options.text: Praise for those who think independently.
options.note: The verse pronounces woe, judgment, not praise, on this moral inversion.

quiz.q: How does the chapter describe the army summoned in verses 26-30?

options.text: Swift, tireless, disciplined, and relentless, like a lion seizing its prey, with no one able to rescue the victims.
options.note: The vivid military imagery emphasizes the certainty and thoroughness of the coming judgment.

options.text: A weak and disorganized rabble easily repelled.
options.note: The description emphasizes overwhelming strength and precision, the opposite of weakness.

options.text: An army that will arrive slowly over many years.
options.note: Verse 26 explicitly says, 'how speedily and swiftly they come.'

options.text: A symbolic army with no real-world referent.
options.note: While the nation is left unnamed, the description matches real historical military campaigns like Assyria's, not a purely symbolic force.

questions: God did everything possible for His vineyard, yet it produced wild grapes. Where has God given you every advantage, and what fruit is your life actually producing in response?
The six woes name specific, concrete sins, greed, drunken indifference, moral confusion, pride, corrupt justice. Which of these hits closest to home for you right now, and why?
Verse 20 warns against calling evil good and good evil. Where are you tempted to relabel something wrong as acceptable because it is common or convenient?
God remained sovereign even over the pagan army He summoned as judgment. What does it mean for your own anxieties to know that no power, however fierce, operates outside God's authority?

Jesus later took up this vineyard image and said the owner finally sent his own son. How does knowing God's patience led all the way to sending Christ change the weight you give to His patience with you now?

translationNotes.note: 'My beloved' can describe a friend, a lover, or a kinsman in Hebrew; the song's opening romantic register makes the abrupt legal turn in verse 3 more jarring by contrast.

The wordplay mishpat, justice, versus mispach, bloodshed, and tzedaqah, righteousness, versus tze'aqah, a cry of distress, is one of the most celebrated examples of Hebrew paronomasia in the prophets, largely untranslatable into English directly.
Sheol is personified with a throat and jaws, vivid imagery for the grave's insatiable appetite, common in ancient Near Eastern poetic descriptions of death.
